job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Zoe Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in a student flat in Hamilton, in New Zealand's Waikato, studying for a master's in applied finance. Mornings are classes, afternoons are bookkeeping for six local farm families and our church, which I do with an AI tool that reads their receipts. I charge 40 dollars an hour, and on a good week it's 12 hours. Sundays I play keyboard in the church band.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a bachelor's in management with an accounting major here, and passed with an average mark. No internship, because the firms wanted people with a connection and I grew up in a town where my dad drives a milk tanker and my mum is the church secretary. I owe about 48,000 dollars. The farm bookkeeping started when a church member's wife was drowning in paperwork, and I used an AI app to sort it out in an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, because the tools are handy but they don't take over. I'd say hard work and being useful to people will keep mattering, and I'd say it at church and at my farm clients' kitchen tables.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pressure stays the same: 48,000 dollars of debt and few accounting jobs in Waikato for someone with an average mark. I do have my farm clients, which is a cushion most graduates don't have. But it's six families, and one bad dairy year could cut my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, apply to ten rural accountancy firms and the farm supply co-ops, and keep growing the farm bookkeeping to about ten clients. I'd put 300 a month on the loan. And I'd keep going to church events, because that's where half my introductions come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but I sleep okay. I've got something of my own to lean on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the farm work lead to a proper job, or just stays side income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I'd hope. A rural firm might hire me because I already know the farmers, and my clients are proof. But if the firms won't, I'd grow it into my own small practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about the debt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm sorry for it, and that I'm working on it. My dad would say not to be sorry, that a debt you work off is honest. My mum would say the Lord provides, and then check my spreadsheet.

Put 300 a month on the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who work hard and keep learning, and I'd tell my church friends not to be afraid of it. I'd also say that good business doesn't need a handout, just a fair field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm nervous about my own edge. The tool I use now is what everyone will have, so farmers could do their own books in a few years. The junior accountancy jobs shrink, and a part-time bookkeeper might be the first thing a farmer cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move up from receipts to advice, like helping farmers plan cash flow, tax and succession. I'd get my accounting qualification so clients trust me, and keep using the tools every day. And I'd apply to rural firms that want someone to serve farmers on the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I like a challenge. It's a bit like a drought year, you plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If farmers can use the tools themselves, what happens to your bookkeeping business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They could. That's the worry. A farmer with a smartphone and a bit of patience can already do half of what I do. So the value has to be advice and trust, not data entry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be your edge over the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being there. I know their families, their loans, which paddock is wet. A tool doesn't come to the farm gate and sit at the kitchen table when someone's father has died and the farm needs a plan.

I'd say good business needs a fair field, not a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to hold together as families and churches, and I'd say governments need to move quickly and not get in the way of people trying to adapt. I'd ask for time, and I'd offer to help others who are struggling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My whole business is thinking work. If AI does that as well and cheaper, then my farmers don't need me, and no firm needs a graduate either. I'd be 26 with 48,000 dollars of debt and a skill that's worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd tell my clients honestly that the tools will replace me, and ask whether I can help them set up and run the tools for the next year. I'd also look for a hands-on job, like on a dairy farm with the church friends, since robots take about three more years. And I'd cut everything extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot, and also making lists, because that's how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that my dad's job driving the tanker has a few more years, which is a strange comfort. I'd say I'm sorry about the debt, and we'd pray together. Then I'd start applying for farm work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your bookkeeping clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with each of the six families and say, here's what I can do for you now, and here's what I can't. Then I'd help them set up the new system and charge for the setup. It's honest, and it's an exit.

say: I'd say we need to **hold together** as families and churches.
I'd say governments must move quickly without blocking people who adapt.
think: My whole business is **thinking work** and could be worthless.
I'd be 26 with 48,000 dollars of debt.

feel: **Alarmed**, praying a lot and making lists to cope.
S2.quote: I'd sit with each of the six families and say, here's what I can do for you now, and here's what I can't.
fieldNote: Even an **early adopter** sees her own work replaced in two years.
Plans an honest **handover** to clients, charging for setup.
Hands-on **dairy work** is her bridge for three extra years.

steps.text: Offer each of my six farm families paid system setup
Look for hands-on work on a dairy farm
Cut every extra expense and track spending weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people don't waste it, and I'd tell young people to start learning something practical. I'd also tell churches to keep an eye out for the families who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be nervous, but I'd have a plan. Five years gets me through the master's, a first job, and a good bite out of the loan. By 2031 I'd be 29 and I'd want to own something, not just be somebody's employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job at a rural firm and treat it as my training year. I'd keep my farm clients and keep adding the advice side. I'd put 400 dollars a month on the loan. And I'd start saving for my own small practice, because a bookkeeper who runs the tools for farmers might survive as an owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but fired up. It feels like a long planting season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to turn my side job into something that doesn't depend on one tool. In two years I'd have no time. In five I could build a farm advisory business that has people trusting me by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What business could you build in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farm advisory practice in the Waikato, with me as the face and the tools doing the number work. I'd charge for judgement and for turning up. If a robot can do the milking, someone still needs to explain the finances to a farmer who's 62 and tired.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to prepare** if people don't waste it.
I'd tell churches to look out for families who lose work.
think: I'd be nervous but have a **plan**: a first job and a bite out of the loan.
I'd want to own something, not just be an employee.

S3.quote: I'd charge for judgement and for turning up.

Put 400 dollars a month on the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift and we should use it with good sense, hard work and care for each other. I'd tell churches and clubs to build things like training and local jobs, not wait for someone else to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, I think. I'd have my own practice, the loan gone, and probably a husband and a child. What I'd keep watching is the people who can't adapt as quickly, like my dad's mates who drive trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work for a rural firm for two or three years, then go out on my own. I'd keep learning the tools as they change, because it's the easiest way to stay ahead. And I'd start a small church fund for people in our community who've lost work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, with a bit of a buzz. I like building things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self about taking on debt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the debt was worth it, but I'd say get a short placement in your first year even if it's unpaid, because it's the one thing every firm asked me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope Waikato looks like in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A town where people still know each other, where farms use the tools but the people stay. I'd like to be one of the folks helping the farmers and the church through it.

I'd tell churches and clubs to build local jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one, because my whole business is thinking work and I'd have debt and no runway. What would help is time, honest warning from leaders and room for people to adapt without red tape.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why I do the farm work. I like the farm work because a stressed farmer relaxes when the books finally add up. It's a small thing, but it matters to me that somebody walks away lighter.

headlineQuote: I like the farm work because a stressed farmer relaxes when the books finally add up.
portrait: Zoe is a **24-year-old** applied finance master's student in Hamilton, New Zealand, owing 48,000 dollars with no internship.
She is **traditional**: values work, faith, community and free markets, and wants room to adapt without red tape.
She is **adaptive**, using AI daily to run bookkeeping for six farm families and her church.
Her mood moves from **uneasy** in quiet worlds to alarmed at 2028, when her whole business is exposed.
Her father drives a **milk tanker** and her mother is a church secretary, so no family money.
biggestWorry: Zoe fears **2028** most, because her whole business is thinking work and she would have no runway.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **time**, honest warning from leaders and room to adapt without red tape.
